title: Minimum Take Home floor is enforceable only when the protected deduction runs last (highest Master Calculation Sequence)
question: Why isn't the Minimum Take Home on my Employee Deduction holding? The deduction is still being taken at its full amount even though the resulting Net Pay drops below the configured floor.
answer: The Minimum Take Home on an Employee Deduction is a floor: it should trim the deduction if enforcing the full deduction amount would push Net Pay below the configured minimum. For this floor to hold reliably, the protected deduction (garnishment, court-ordered deduction, priority employer contribution, or any deduction with a Minimum Take Home configured) MUST have a Master Calculation Sequence HIGHER than every other deduction and tax that reduces Net Pay for the affected employees. Functionally: the floor is enforced at the moment the deduction is calculated, so the system needs the deduction to be evaluated AFTER every other reduction has run — otherwise the calculation cannot reserve the floor from the protected deduction's vantage point. Setting the protected deduction to a very high sequence (e.g. 99999) ensures it processes last and the floor can be enforced. Empirically confirmed via side-by-side test on the same employee (SAM002), same Percentage type deduction at 50%, same $217.50 Minimum Take Home, same $400 gross wages, same tax deductions: Master Calculation Sequence = 12 produced Net Pay = $143.48 — the floor did NOT hold and the deduction ran at its full natural amount ($200); Master Calculation Sequence = 99999 produced Net Pay = exactly $217.50 — the floor held and the deduction was trimmed from $200 to $125.98 to preserve the minimum. The only variable that differed between the two runs was the Master Calculation Sequence.

reviewer_notes: This finding is empirically strong — two side-by-side analyst tests on case 00618659 (C1 Garnishment) where the only variable was Master Calculation Sequence (12 vs 99999) and the outcome flipped from floor-fails to floor-holds. However, the exact runtime mechanic ('the floor is checked at the moment the deduction is calculated, so all other reductions must have already run') is INFERRED from the observed behaviour, not from an explicit statement in the current library. A silent source-code check would pin down the exact runtime spec — recommend running one as part of verification. If source confirms the inferred mechanic, this finding can be published to the library as a clear rule. If source contradicts it, the finding should be revised before publishing.
